usage: Warmer and more heartfelt than 아주; natural when talking about people or feelings
Adds genuine emotional weight; sounds sincere, not exaggerated
Works for weather and physical states; more expressive than a flat 아주
The -이나 suffix adds extra emphasis and a slightly literary, emotional tone
examples: 저 사람 무척 친절해요.
That person is really kind.
Simple subject + 무척 + adjective; notice 무척 sits right before the describing word
한국 음식이 무척 입에 맞아요.
Korean food really suits my taste.
입에 맞다 (lit. 'fit the mouth') is the set phrase for food agreeing with you
그 소식을 듣고 무척 놀랐어요.
I was really surprised to hear that news.
Pairs naturally with emotion verbs like 놀라다, 기뻐하다, 슬퍼하다
nuance: 무척 means 'very/really,' but unlike the neutral, almost clinical 아주, it carries a warm emotional undertone, so it gravitates toward feelings, people, and personal reactions rather than dry measurements. The dividing line with 아주: you would say 아주 정확하다 (very precise — a cool fact) but 무척 그립다 (miss someone terribly — a feeling). Register is soft and slightly literary, fully standard and never rude, so it works in heartfelt speech and writing alike; in fast texting younger Koreans swap in 너무 or 진짜. The English-speaker pitfall is using it for negation: English 'not very' does NOT become 무척 안 — Korean wants 그다지 안 or 별로 안 there, because 무척 only intensifies upward.

Unlike the neutral, almost clinical 아주, 무척 is warm. The dividing line: you would say 아주 정확하다 (very precise — a cool fact) but 무척 그립다 (miss someone terribly — a feeling).
The pitfall is using it for negation: English 'not very' does NOT become 무척 안 — Korean wants 그다지 안 or 별로 안 there, because 무척 only intensifies upward.

mistakes: Saying 무척 안 좋아요 for 'not very good' — 무척 only pushes a degree higher, so for 'not very' you need 별로 안 좋아요 or 그다지 좋지 않아요.
Treating 무척 as slang to avoid in polite settings; it is fully standard and soft/literary, so it never sounds rude or too casual even with a boss.
Forcing it onto cold technical facts (무척 정확하다); the emotional flavor clashes, and 아주/매우 정확하다 sounds far more natural there.

usage: Everyday strong intensifier, a clear notch above 아주
Loves words of size, scale, amount, or impressiveness
Expresses genuine surprise at a high degree
The base adjective stands alone: 우와, 굉장하다! = Wow, amazing!
examples: 이 가방 굉장히 가벼워요.
This bag is incredibly light.
Simple form; 굉장히 directly modifies the adjective 가볍다
면접 준비를 굉장히 열심히 했어요.
I prepared incredibly hard for the interview.
Here it stacks onto the adverb 열심히 to stress effort
오늘 지하철이 굉장히 붐비네요.
The subway is extremely crowded today.
붐비다 = to be crowded; a natural commuter remark with -네요 surprise
nuance: 굉장히 is one of the most accessible STRONG intensifiers in everyday Korean and sounds natural in both casual chat and polite speech, even work emails. It comes from the hanja 宏壯 (굉장: 宏 'vast' + 壯 'magnificent') plus the adverbial -히, so at its root it paints something as grand or imposing — which is why it shines on scale and impressiveness (굉장히 크다/많다/대단하다). The synonym line: it overlaps with the breezier, more colloquial 엄청, but 굉장히 is a touch more composed and presentable, while 엄청 is punchier and more slang-leaning. Two English-speaker pitfalls: spelling (it is 굉장히 with 히, never 굉장이), and proportion — slapping 굉장히 on a trivial thing sounds like overstatement, where 꽤 or 좀 fits better.

mistakes: Writing 굉장이 — the adverb is always 굉장히 (adjective stem 굉장 + -히); 굉장이 is simply a misspelling.
Overusing it on minor things (굉장히 for a tiny inconvenience); that reads as exaggeration, and 꽤 or 좀 would sound calmer and more natural.
Assuming the hanja meaning 'grand' lets it modify nouns like 상당한 does; 굉장히 is purely an adverb, so before a noun you must use the adjective form 굉장한 (굉장한 인기).

usage: Measured and slightly formal; common in reviews and reports
Polished tone, good for feedback and workplace talk
Adnominal form 상당한: 상당한 시간 = a considerable amount of time
examples: 이 식당, 가격이 상당히 괜찮아요.
This restaurant's prices are quite reasonable.
Everyday-but-composed; 상당히 keeps the tone objective
그 동네는 월세가 상당히 높은 편이에요.
Rents in that neighborhood are considerably high.
-은 편이다 = 'tends to be,' softening the claim into a measured observation
이번 프로젝트가 상당히 까다로웠어요.
This project was considerably tricky.
Sounds professional and controlled in a work debrief
nuance: 상당히 marks a notable, MEASURED degree and carries a composed, semi-formal tone, so it lives in reviews, reports, and adult conversation. Its hanja 相當 (相 'mutual' + 當 'corresponding/befitting') literally means 'matching/befitting an amount' — i.e. 'amounting to a fair bit,' which is exactly why it feels objective, like you are reporting a fact rather than emoting. Synonym contrast: against the emotional 무척 or the casual 되게, 상당히 sounds understated and analytical; against 꽤 (also 'quite'), 상당히 is a touch stronger and more written-sounding. The key English-speaker pitfall is the adverb-vs-adnominal split: use 상당히 directly before a verb/adjective (상당히 어렵다), but switch to 상당한 directly before a noun (상당한 노력) — you cannot say 상당히 노력 as a noun phrase.

mistakes: Using it in very casual chat with close friends, where it sounds stiff and bookish — 되게 or 엄청 land far more naturally there.
Confusing the adverb 상당히 with the adnominal 상당한; before a noun you must say 상당한 (상당한 시간/노력), not 상당히 시간.
Reading it as purely emotional 'very'; 상당히 signals an objective, fair-sized degree, so pairing it with gushing feelings (상당히 사랑해요) sounds oddly detached.

usage: You're pretty good (better than I expected)
Notes that something has actually reached a real degree
Stands alone as praise: 오, 제법인데? = Oh, not bad!
examples: 어, 너 요리 제법 하는데?
Oh, you can actually cook pretty well!
Casual 반말; 제법 carries the 'I didn't expect this' surprise
아침저녁으로 제법 쌀쌀해졌어요.
It's gotten fairly chilly morning and evening.
쌀쌀하다 = chilly; classic autumn small talk with -아졌어요 'has become'
이 식당, 가격은 싼데 맛은 제법이에요.
This place is cheap but the food is actually quite good.
Shows the core nuance: the result beats the low price expectation
nuance: 제법 means 'fairly/quite,' but its defining flavor is that something turned out BETTER or MORE than you expected, usually with a dash of admiration. That expectation gap is the whole point: 제법 잘하네요 is a warm compliment ('better than I thought!'), whereas a flat 잘하네요 is neutral praise, and a strong 아주 잘하네요 just rates a high level with no surprise. Synonym contrast: 꽤 also means 'quite/fairly' but is emotionally neutral about expectation, while 제법 specifically encodes 'pleasantly surprising.' Register is friendly and conversational. The English-speaker pitfall is social: because it implies 'I didn't expect you to be this good,' aiming 제법 at a clear expert or a respected senior can sound faintly patronizing — praise them with 정말/아주 instead.

Applying it to things you always knew would be good (제법 맛있는 유명 맛집); with no surprise gap the word loses its point and sounds off.

usage: Formal softening tone for notices and emails
Common in reports and official announcements
Diplomatic way to express mild disappointment
examples: 오늘은 바람이 다소 강하겠습니다.
Today the wind will be somewhat strong.
Pure weather-forecast register; the -겠습니다 ending matches the formal tone
배송이 다소 지연되어 죄송합니다.
We apologize that the delivery is somewhat delayed.
Standard wording in shop and delivery notices; softens the bad news
설명이 다소 복잡하니 천천히 읽어 주세요.
The explanation is rather complex, so please read it slowly.
A polite hedge inside instructions, lowering the alarm
nuance: 다소 means 'somewhat / a little,' but it belongs squarely to FORMAL written and broadcast Korean — notices, weather reports, customer messages, official statements — not chatting with friends. Its hanja 多少 (多 'many' + 少 'few') literally pairs 'more-or-less,' giving it the cool, hedging feel of English 'somewhat,' and it gravitates to mildly negative partners (다소 지연/부족/아쉽다) to soften the blow politely. Synonym contrast: 다소 and 약간 both mean 'slightly,' but 약간 is everyday-neutral and 다소 is buttoned-up and bureaucratic; in casual speech Koreans simply say 좀 or 약간. The English-speaker pitfall is register mismatch and over-stacking: dropping 다소 into friendly chat sounds stiff, and because it means a SMALL-to-moderate degree, combining it with a strong word (다소 엄청) is self-contradictory.

mistakes: Using 다소 in casual conversation with friends; it sounds oddly formal and newscaster-like — use 좀 or 약간 instead.
Pairing it with strong intensifiers (다소 엄청 / 다소 매우); 다소 caps the degree at small-to-moderate, so it contradicts a 'very' word.
Assuming it carries warmth like English 'a bit'; 다소 is detached and official, so for soft, friendly understatement 살짝 or 좀 fits better.

usage: Very common for taste, temperature, and feelings
Cooking instruction: only briefly in hot water
Please open the door just a bit
Describes a small, gentle physical action
Softens an emotion in a cute, casual way
examples: 국이 살짝 싱거워요.
The soup is slightly bland.
싱겁다 = bland; the simplest taste use, 살짝 + adjective
여기 좀 살짝 비켜 주실래요?
Could you move over just a little here?
살짝 makes the request gentle and low-pressure for an action verb
가격이 살짝 부담되긴 해요.
The price is a touch burdensome, honestly.
살짝 softens the complaint; -긴 하다 adds 'admittedly'
nuance: 살짝 means 'slightly,' but with a light, gentle, often cute texture, and crucially it modifies ACTIONS as much as states — doing something briefly, softly, or by a small amount (살짝 만지다 'touch lightly,' 살짝 웃다 'smile faintly'). It is hugely common in casual speech and cooking. Synonym contrast with 약간: 약간 is the neutral, measurable 'a little' (약간 차이가 난다), whereas 살짝 is vivid, conversational, and tactile — 'just a touch,' often implying a quick, delicate motion. The big English-speaker pitfall is mentally filing it under 'somewhat' only and forgetting the action sense: English 'slightly' rarely describes how you do something, but 살짝 happily does (살짝 닫다 = close gently), so do not restrict it to adjectives. It also only ever means SMALL — never use it for big degrees.

Forgetting it modifies actions, not just adjectives; 살짝 만지다 means 'touch lightly' and 살짝 열다 'open a crack' — it is not purely a 'somewhat' word.
Swapping in the formal 다소 in friendly chat to mean the same thing; 살짝 is warm and casual, while 다소 sounds like a press release.

usage: Must pair with a negative; stresses total inability
I just can't understand it at all
이해가 안 가다 = it doesn't make sense to me
It just won't work no matter what
잠이 안 오다 = sleep won't come
examples: 이게 도무지 무슨 말인지 모르겠어요.
I simply can't tell what this even means.
Basic frame: 도무지 ... 모르겠다, the textbook 'can't grasp it' use
요즘 일이 많아서 도무지 시간이 안 나요.
I'm so busy lately that I just can't find any time.
시간이 나다 = to have time free; the 안 is what 도무지 leans on
몇 번을 봐도 도무지 답을 모르겠어요.
No matter how many times I look, I just can't get the answer.
몇 번을 봐도 = 'however many times I look,' amplifying the helplessness
nuance: 도무지 means 'not at all / simply (cannot)' and is a NEGATIVE-POLARITY adverb: it must be answered later in the sentence by a negative (안, 못, 모르다, -지 않다), and it adds a strong color of frustration and total impossibility, very often about failing to understand or grasp something. Synonym contrast: it is nearly interchangeable with 도저히, but 도저히 leans 'there is no way / it can't be done however hard I try' (도저히 못 참겠다), while 도무지 leans 'I simply can't make sense of it,' tilting toward confusion. Do NOT confuse it with the look-alike 도대체, which is an interrogative intensifier meaning 'what on earth?' (도대체 왜?) and questions rather than negates. The headline English-speaker pitfall: because English 'simply' can be positive, learners write 도무지 좋아요, which is impossible — 도무지 cannot appear in an affirmative sentence at all.

Swapping it freely with 전혀; 전혀 is a neutral 'not at all' for any negated fact (전혀 안 맵다), whereas 도무지 specifically adds frustrated 'no matter what I do' inability.

usage: Almost always with a comparison; frequently sits before 더
Stresses a big gap between two things
버스보다 훨씬 빨라요 = much faster than the bus
낫다 → 나아요; common when comparing conditions or states
examples: 이게 저것보다 훨씬 싸요.
This is far cheaper than that one.
The bare A보다 B 훨씬 frame; 훨씬 marks how big the price gap is
약 먹고 나니까 훨씬 괜찮아졌어요.
After taking the medicine, I feel much better.
괜찮아지다 = to get better; comparison is implied between before and after
이 집이 전에 살던 곳보다 훨씬 넓어요.
This place is far more spacious than where I lived before.
보다 names the thing compared; 훨씬 says the difference is large
nuance: 훨씬 is the go-to word for emphasizing a LARGE gap in a comparison — 'much/far more' — and it implies the difference is significant, not slight. It pairs naturally with 더 (훨씬 더 빠르다) and with the 보다 comparative structure (택시보다 훨씬). The crucial contrast is with general intensifiers: 아주/너무 just rate one thing's degree on its own ('very fast'), but 훨씬 is inherently RELATIVE and needs a second thing to measure against ('much faster than X'). It also differs from 더 alone, which says merely 'more' with no claim about size, while 훨씬 insists the gap is big. The English-speaker pitfall: 'much better' tempts you to say 훨씬 좋아요 in isolation, but with no expressed or implied 'than what?' it sounds incomplete — Korean expects a comparison target, even if context supplies it.

mistakes: Using 훨씬 with no comparison at all (훨씬 좋아요 out of nowhere); it is comparative, so there must be an expressed or clearly implied 'than X.'
Replacing 아주/너무 with 훨씬 for a simple high degree; 훨씬 specifically means 'by a large margin more,' not a general 'very.'
Dropping 더 where the meaning is 'more' and expecting 훨씬 alone to carry it in subtle cases; 훨씬 더 is the safe, natural pairing for 'much more.'

usage: Super common in casual speech, like a spoken 'really'
Everyday complaint about distance or effort
Mainly spoken; in writing people prefer 정말/아주
examples: 오늘 되게 더워요.
It's so hot today.
The simplest pattern: 되게 + adjective in casual 해요-speech
여기 분위기 되게 좋다, 자주 오자.
This place has a really nice vibe, let's come often.
분위기 = vibe; pure 반말 among friends, where 되게 thrives
오늘 길이 되게 막히네요.
The roads are really jammed today.
막히다 = to be congested; an everyday gripe with -네요
nuance: 되게 is a very common CASUAL intensifier meaning 'really/so,' used almost exclusively in spoken Korean among friends, peers, and people you are comfortable with. It feels lively and effortless in conversation but looks out of place in formal writing or business email, where 아주, 매우, or 정말 belong. Synonym contrast: it sits right beside 엄청 and 진짜 as spoken boosters, but 되게 is the most conversational and a bit softer than the punchy 엄청; meaning-wise it just means 'very,' with none of the 'large amount' flavor 엄청 can carry. Two English-speaker pitfalls: spelling and register. Spelling — it is 되게 (from 되다), never 됬게 or 돼게, since 되 + 게 takes no extra ㅆ. Register — because it is so casual, using it in anything written or official instantly sounds too chatty.

Two pitfalls: spelling and register. Spelling — it is 되게 (from 되다), never 됬게 or 돼게, since 되 + 게 takes no extra ㅆ. Register — because it is so casual, using it in anything written or official instantly sounds too chatty.

mistakes: Writing 되게 in formal documents, emails, or reports, where it reads as too casual; use 매우/정말/아주 in those registers.
Spelling it 됬게 or 돼게; the correct form is 되게 (stem 되- + -게), with no doubled ㅆ and no 돼.
Assuming it means 'a lot/a ton' like 엄청 can for quantity; 되게 only intensifies a quality ('very'), so 되게 많이 is fine but 되게 alone won't carry 'a huge amount.'

usage: Strong and casual; great for amounts and intensity alike
Common spoken intensifier across all ages
Adjective form: 효과가 엄청나요 = the effect is huge
examples: 사람이 엄청 많아요.
There are a ton of people.
Quantity use; 엄청 + 많다 is the most natural high-amount pairing
이번 시험 공부를 엄청 했는데 떨려요.
I studied a ton for this exam but I'm nervous.
떨리다 = to feel nervous/shaky; 엄청 here measures the effort
배달이 엄청 빨리 왔어요.
The delivery came incredibly fast.
엄청 stacks onto the adverb 빨리; a classic food-delivery comment
nuance: 엄청 is a punchy, casual way to say 'super / a ton,' and it is unusual among these adverbs in handling both QUANTITY (엄청 많다 'a ton') and INTENSITY (엄청 덥다 'super hot') with equal ease. Register is colloquial — extremely frequent in speech and texting across all ages, a step less formal than 굉장히 and far less formal than 매우/대단히. Synonym contrast: against 굉장히, 엄청 is breezier and more slang-flavored while 굉장히 sounds more presentable; against 되게, 엄청 hits harder and can carry the 'huge amount' sense that 되게 cannot. A handy feature is the adjective spin-off 엄청나다 ('to be tremendous') and its adverb 엄청나게, letting you say 효과가 엄청나요. The English-speaker pitfall is degree: like all strong boosters it means a genuinely LARGE amount, so using it for something small (엄청 for a tiny bit) is wrong — reach for 살짝/약간 there.

usage: Often paired with 더; pictures stepping up one level
Common in product and service descriptions
Slightly formal; used for improvement and progress
Nice for relationships deepening one notch
examples: 봄이 되니 날이 한층 따뜻해졌어요.
Now that it's spring, the days have gotten even warmer.
한층 + 더 implied; the 'one step up from before' feel is built in
연습을 꾸준히 했더니 실력이 한층 늘었어요.
Since I practiced steadily, my skills improved even further.
한층 stresses a clear step up from an existing level
가을이 되니 단풍이 한층 아름다워요.
Now that it's autumn, the foliage is even more beautiful.
단풍 = autumn leaves; the slightly literary tone suits 한층
nuance: 한층 means 'even more / a level higher,' and it literally pictures improvement as climbing one more 층 (層, 'floor/story/layer') above an already-good state — that built-in 'from an existing baseline, step up one' is its core. Because of that, it almost always implies a POSITIVE upgrade and frequently appears as 한층 더 for extra force. Register is polished and a little written-sounding, so it suits reviews, product copy, and thoughtful speech more than rapid 반말. Synonym contrast: against plain 더 ('more,' no baseline assumption) 한층 insists there was already a good level you are now exceeding; against 훨씬 ('much more,' comparing two separate things by a big margin) 한층 is about one thing rising another step over its former self, and the rise can be modest. The English-speaker pitfall: do not use 한층 for a first-time, baseline-less degree (it needs a prior state to step up from), and in casual chat a simple 더 or 훨씬 usually sounds more natural.

usage: Implies a sudden, visible rise over a short time
Notes a marked change in someone's appearance
부쩍 자주 보이네요 = I see you around a lot more lately
examples: 요즘 부쩍 피곤해요.
I've been noticeably more tired lately.
요즘 + 부쩍 is the textbook pairing for a recent, striking change
환절기라 그런지 감기 환자가 부쩍 늘었어요.
Maybe because of the season change, cold patients have increased markedly.
환절기 = change of seasons; 늘다 is the change verb 부쩍 loves
조카가 못 본 사이에 부쩍 컸어요.
My niece/nephew has grown so much since I last saw them.
못 본 사이에 = 'while I wasn't seeing them'; stresses the jump you suddenly notice
nuance: 부쩍 describes a MARKED, noticeable change that happened over a relatively short stretch — 'suddenly a lot more' — and it is a native Korean (non-Sino) word with a vivid, observational feel. Grammatically it craves VERBS OF CHANGE (늘다, 줄다, 커지다, 추워지다, 늙다) rather than static adjectives, and it pairs constantly with 요즘 to mean 'lately, and you can really tell.' The key synonym contrast is with 점점 and 차츰: those describe GRADUAL, step-by-step change ('more and more, slowly'), whereas 부쩍 stresses that the jump was striking and easy to notice, almost abrupt. The English-speaker pitfall: because English 'noticeably' attaches happily to adjectives ('noticeably pretty'), learners try 부쩍 예쁘다, which sounds odd — Korean wants the change form 부쩍 예뻐졌다 ('got noticeably prettier'), since 부쩍 is about movement to a new state, not a static quality.
